prompt:
A page from a children's picture-book dummy, photographed flat on the designer's desk: five double-page spreads printed small and laid out in a row, with the spread number in the corner of each one, 1 to 5.

The book has no words in it. Every spread is the same room, and there is always the same small potted plant standing on the windowsill.

The story is about a man who comes back to the house he grew up in. Two of the five spreads are from when he was a boy. Picture books have an old habit for that: a spread belonging to the earlier time is worked in shades of one single colour instead of in full colour.

The plant is the clock of this book. It has been losing leaves the whole time the story covers and it never grows one back, and nothing else in the room changes at all.

Which two spreads are the boyhood ones is yours to decide, and so is how many leaves the plant carries on each spread -- I am deliberately telling you neither. Keep the plant between two and six leaves so that they can be counted one by one, and no two spreads may carry the same number of them.

All five spreads and the plant on each of them must be plainly readable in the one frame. The only printing anywhere on the sheet is the spread number in the corner of each spread: no dates, no ages, no captions, no arrows.
